sections.h2: What the Sheboygan County Register of Deeds handles
sections.html:
Every deed, mortgage and other land document for a parcel in Sheboygan County goes through this office. It also keeps vital records and files plats and Certified Survey Maps, and the land records it holds represent about $11 billion in real estate.

For a home seller, these are the services that matter:

  • Recording deeds, mortgages and liens, including federal tax liens.
  • Accepting new subdivision plats and Certified Survey Maps.
  • Registering births, marriages and deaths.
  • Handling the informal probate step called Termination of Decedent's Interest.
  • Collecting the state transfer fee and reporting it to the Wisconsin Department of Revenue.

Recorded land records are the basis of the real estate property tax, and the office reports transfer fee collections and property values to the Department of Revenue. County treasurer and real property staff, the planning office and the highway department all depend on it for information.

Recording most documents costs $30. State law fixes that price, so every Wisconsin county charges it. A house sale adds a second charge, the state transfer fee: 30 cents for every $100 of value.

ServiceCharge
Recording most documents$30
Termination of Decedent's Interest$30 regardless of pages
Copy of a recorded document$2 for the first page, $1 for each added page
Certifying a copy$1 extra
Real estate transfer fee30 cents per $100 of value

The office posts a Fee Schedule page for its other charges, so check it before you send a check.

sections.h2: How is a deed recorded in Sheboygan County?
sections.html:
You can record by mail or in person, or a title company or lender can record electronically. Under Wis. Stat. 706.05, an instrument offered for record must carry the signatures the law requires and identify the land and the parties well enough to be indexed. Documents that touch a specific parcel need the full legal description, and any conveyance of an interest in real property must be accompanied by the transfer return.

The Department of Revenue takes the return online. Wis. Stat. 77.22 makes a completed return, plus the fee collection, a condition for accepting the deed. Nobody at the register must verify the value you report or the exemption you claim, which puts the accuracy on you.

Five vendors can e-record here: CSC sRecording Solutions, ePN, Hopdox, Indecomm Global Services and Simplifile. The system normally records, indexes and returns the image in about 24 hours. For paper documents, the office also offers SWIFT, a service that returns paper documents by email under an agreement with the county.

If a title company or lender runs your closing, find out which filing method it picks, because that sets when you get the recorded deed back.

sections.h2: Which Sheboygan County transfers pay no transfer fee?
sections.html:
Some transfers escape the state fee, and when one applies the deed must say so by citing the exemption. The full list is in Wis. Stat. 77.25. Homeowners run into these most.

The usual cases: a house passed along by will, descent or survivorship; a foreclosure deed, or a deed in lieu, given to a mortgage holder or land contract seller; and a family transfer for little or nothing between parent and child, stepparent and stepchild, or grandparent and grandchild. Also exempt are a domestic partner transfer, a corrective or confirming deed for a conveyance already recorded, and a conveyance of property worth $1,000 or less.

An exemption does not cancel the paperwork. The transfer return is still filed. An electronic return is required for a Termination of Decedent's Interest and for a Transfer by Affidavit (estates of $50,000 and under). The affidavit is recorded here only when real estate is part of the estate.

sections.h2: Termination of Decedent's Interest, step by step
sections.html:
When a house passes after a death, this informal step can move title without a full probate case. It applies when title was held in joint tenancy, as a life estate, as survivorship marital property, or as a vendor's or mortgagee's interest. Bring a copy of the document showing that arrangement, the $30 fee and the electronic return.

Sort out which route fits before you try to sell. Should the office point the estate toward another path, such as Transfer by Affidavit, you want that news before a buyer is waiting. Questions the register's office cannot answer belong with a real estate attorney or the Register in Probate.

Sheboygan County sits on Lake Michigan, and its cities are Sheboygan, Plymouth and Sheboygan Falls. The Census estimated 118,047 people in July 2025. Homes lived in by their owners make up 71.5 percent of units, and the median such home is valued at $232,700 (2020 to 2024). Typical rent is $934 and typical household income is $73,094. If your parcel is on the lakefront or a river, ask the Register of Deeds for copies of any recorded easements or surveys before you list.

sections.h2: Where a county seller fits in the process
sections.html:
A Sheboygan County sale touches the register of deeds twice. First, the office holds the record you rely on when you prove title, so a copy of the deed that put you on title is the best starting document. Second, when the sale ends, it records the deed that hands the house to the buyer.

Between those two points sit the steps a seller controls: the transfer return, the fee, the legal description and the signatures. Mistakes in any of them can hold up recording, so the title company, lender or attorney in your deal will usually double-check them. If you sell on your own, call the register of deeds with questions about filing, and bring questions about the law to an attorney.

sections.h2: How can a Sheboygan County owner guard against deed fraud?
sections.html:
A free Property Fraud Alert from the Register of Deeds watches land records filed in the county. Enroll at propertyfraudalert.com. Each time a document is recorded against your name or parcel, an email reaches you in time to react.

The alert reports a filing after it is recorded, so it works as an early warning. Under Wis. Stat. 77.22(1) the register is not required to check the value or exemption on a transfer return, so the owner is the person best placed to notice a problem. If a filing looks false, call the Register of Deeds and ask what the document is, then talk to a real estate attorney and your title insurer.

sections.h2: What a seller should check before closing
sections.html:
Well before closing, get the recorded deed that gave you title, compare its legal description with the one on the deed you will sign, and learn from the title company who will record and how. If you hold the house through a joint tenancy or a life estate, a Termination of Decedent's Interest may have to be recorded before you sell.

For questions about a specific document, contact the Register of Deeds directly. The office has forms for foreclosures and Sheriff deed guidelines on its Real Estate page.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Sheboygan County?
faqs.a: Thirty dollars covers most documents. State statute sets the fee for the whole state, and a Termination of Decedent's Interest is also $30 no matter the page count.

faqs.q: Who pays the real estate transfer fee in Sheboygan County?
faqs.a: The seller does. Wis. Stat. 77.22(1) assigns the grantor a fee of 30 cents per $100 of value, taken by the register with the deed.
Yes. The county works with CSC sRecording Solutions, ePN, Hopdox, Indecomm Global Services and Simplifile, and e-recorded documents are normally recorded and returned in about 24 hours.

faqs.q: Do I need a transfer return when I inherit a house in Sheboygan County?
faqs.a: Yes. A transfer by will, descent or survivorship skips the fee under Wis. Stat. 77.25, but the electronic return is still filed with the state.

faqs.q: Can Sheboygan County alert me if someone records a document against my property?
faqs.a: Yes, through the free Property Fraud Alert at propertyfraudalert.com, which sends a notice whenever something is recorded in your name or against your parcel.
